blocks.text: Dear Mr. Vasquez:

Thank you for the morning in your office. It was a candid conversation, more candid than most first meetings are, and we came away understanding why this seat has been hard to fill rather than simply that it has been. We would be glad to run the search. This letter sets down what we have agreed, so that in October neither of us is working from memory.
Please read it against what we discussed. If any part of it sits differently from what you understood, say so before you sign. We will put it right.
The Search We Will Run

Northgate will conduct a retained search for a head of operations at {{fact:f:E-2018-001.client}}, reporting to you. The role is defined by a written position specification. We draft it with you, you approve it, and nobody is approached before you do. It is the document every conversation is then measured against. If the market disagrees with it, and on a role of this kind the market usually has an opinion, we bring that back to you and change the specification openly instead of quietly widening the brief.

Retained is not the same thing as contingent, and the difference shows up in how we behave. What you are buying is the whole market looked at properly, including the parts of it that turn out to hold nobody. A search run this way gives you fewer names and better ones.
How It Proceeds
The work moves through five steps. In practice they overlap, and research carries on while the first approaches are already out.

items: 1. Specification. We meet you and the people this person will work with daily, then draft the specification for your approval.
2. Research. We map the businesses where an operator of this description sits today, and we build the target list off that map.
3. Approach. We make the calls ourselves. Nobody at your company has to have an awkward conversation with a competitor.
4. Slate. We put a short list in front of you with a written appraisal of each person on it, and we run your interview process from there.
5. References and close. We take references in depth, help you shape the offer, and stay with the search until your candidate has accepted and given notice.

blocks.text: You will hear from us on a regular cycle and not only when there is good news to report. Each report tells you how many people we have approached, how many are in live conversation, and where the market is pushing back. Where it pushes back on the specification, you will hear that early, while there is still time to do something with it.
The People On It

James Grant will carry the search day to day and is the person to call about anything of substance. He has spent most of his career on operations roles in owner-managed businesses, and he will not put a name in front of you until he can say precisely why it belongs there. Nicole Donovan handles the research behind the target list, the scheduling, and the written record of our sessions with you. I read everything that leaves this firm under our name, and my line stays open to you for the length of the search.
Our Fee, and When It Falls Due

The fee for the assignment is {{fact:f:E-2018-001.fee}}. It is fixed at the outset. It is not a percentage of what you eventually agree to pay the person we find, which is what makes our advice on that number worth having. We invoice in three equal parts: on commencement, on delivery of the slate, and on acceptance. Invoices are payable thirty days from receipt.

Expenses sit outside the fee and are billed at cost. They are candidate travel, our own travel to your sites, and any research we buy in from outside the firm. Anything material we agree with you before we incur it. The detail appears line by line on the invoice and never as a lump.
Term, and How Either of Us Ends It

The engagement begins {{fact:f:E-2018-001.start}} and we expect it to run about five months from that point through to a signed acceptance. Either of us may end it on thirty days' written notice. If you end it, you owe the installments already due and the expenses already committed on your behalf. Nothing beyond that.
If the person we place leaves you inside twelve months, for any reason other than a change you make to the role or to its terms, we will run one replacement search for expenses only.
Discretion

What we learn about {{fact:f:E-2018-001.client}} in the course of this work we hold in confidence and use for this search only. We ask the same of you about candidates, and here I will press the point. Most of the people we approach are settled where they are and take a real risk in talking to us at all. Their names stay inside your interview process. They do not appear in board papers or in anything that circulates, and we will not confirm to anyone outside the process that a particular person is in conversation with you.
For the term of this engagement and for one year after it closes, we will not approach the person we place, or anyone on your management team, on behalf of another client.
What We Warrant, and What We Do Not

We will do the work with the care and skill you are entitled to expect. We verify what a candidate tells us about their record, and where something could not be verified we will say so plainly rather than leave it to be assumed. The decision to hire is yours. We give no warranty as to how anyone you employ will perform in the role. Our liability under this agreement is limited to the fees paid under it, except where the law does not permit that limit.
Which Law Governs

This agreement is governed by the law of the state in which our office is established, and any dispute arising under it belongs in that state's courts. If a provision of this letter is found unenforceable, the remainder stands.

If this reflects your understanding, please sign both copies and return one to me. The next step is ours and it is a short one: James Grant will telephone your office this week to fix the two specification meetings, and we would ask you to bring whoever holds the operating numbers today into the second of them.

To: Nicole Donovan
From: James Grant, Senior Consultant
Re: Head of operations search for {{fact:f:E-2018-001.client}}, opening plan and division of work

The engagement commenced {{fact:f:E-2018-001.start}} and is scoped to run about five months, which is enough time to do this properly once and not enough to do it twice, so the opening weeks decide the search. Jason Vasquez is our client on the assignment and the role reports to him. He believes the previous appointment into the seat was recruited out of the wrong industry, and he has said he is willing to be argued with on that point provided the argument arrives with evidence behind it.

The objective for the first six weeks is narrow, and I would rather we hold it narrow than let it broaden by drift: an approved specification, a target list we are prepared to defend, and a compensation band settled in writing before a single approach goes out, because an operator at this level asks about money in the second conversation and a vague answer at that moment costs us the candidate.
The lines of work, and who holds each

items: 1. Specification. I run both sessions on site and draft the specification off them. Nicole Donovan sits in on both and keeps the record. I want an approved draft back from Jason Vasquez inside three weeks of the second session.

2. Market map. Nicole Donovan builds it: the businesses at and just above this scale that have taken an operation through the kind of tightening the client is describing, and the titles inside them where a person of this description would sit today.
3. Compensation. We need a band we can quote without hedging. I put the question in the first session and I hold the client to a figure in writing before the first approach, not after the fourth.
4. Approaches. Mine to make. Nicole Donovan tracks who was approached, when, by what route, and what came back, and that record is the substance of the report the client sees.
5. Assessment. Everyone who reaches a second conversation gets a written appraisal from me before they go anywhere near a slate, and nobody reaches the slate without one.

blocks.text: Two things can cost us the schedule and both of them are early. The first is the specification sitting unapproved on a desk through the middle of the summer while the client travels, which is why I want both sessions inside the fortnight rather than at the end of the month. The second is a band set below what the market will bear, which we would not discover until the fourth or fifth approach came back the same way, by which point we would have spent the names we most wanted on a proposition that could not carry them.
What we do not put in writing

Nothing that circulates carries a candidate's name until that candidate has told their own household and is ready for the conversation to be real. In the fortnightly report, in the minutes of our sessions, and in anything that goes to {{fact:f:E-2018-001.client}} by email, people are described by the role they hold now and the scale of the operation they run. That is not only a courtesy to the candidate; in a market this small one leak ends a search, and it usually ends it before anybody understands that it has.
The first thing that happens

Nicole Donovan calls the client's office tomorrow for two dates inside the next fortnight, and I want the second session to include a walk through the operation itself rather than another hour in a conference room.
Hello Jason,

The specification has been approved on your side for a fortnight now and the first approaches are out, so I am starting this thread to keep the running record of the search in one place; I will send the substantive updates here and keep Nicole copied, since she holds the research and the calendar between us.

Where it stands this morning: the map runs to thirty-one businesses, we have approached nineteen people off it, and eleven of those are in live conversation. Four of the eleven are worth your attention already. I am describing them to you by the operation they run rather than by name until each of them has spoken to their own family and is ready for this to be real, which is the discipline we agreed and the reason people take our calls at all.

Two things from your side would help the pace. Nicole is looking for ninety minutes in your diary in the next fortnight for a calibration session, where we take you through the map and test the specification against what the market has actually said back to us; and three of the businesses on the target list sell into the same accounts as {{fact:f:E-2018-001.client}}, so I need your ruling on whether they are open to us or off limits before the second wave goes out.
If you can give me that ruling by the end of next week, the second wave goes out the week after.
Regards
Hi Jason,

The calibration session is the item with the tighter deadline, so I have gone ahead and held three ninety-minute windows at our end, all of them in the week after next, and your assistant has them from me this morning. Whichever one you take, we come to you.

One correction to James's note yesterday. The eleventh conversation closed overnight, so we are at ten live rather than eleven, and the person stepped back for reasons of their own that have nothing to do with the role or with {{fact:f:E-2018-001.client}}. James will cover it properly at the session.
On the three businesses James raised, nothing goes out to any of them until your ruling reaches us, and I have marked them held on our side so there is no chance of a call being made by accident.

The agenda is one page and it comes to you the day before, so the time in the room goes on the map rather than on catching up. If none of the three windows hold, tell me the day that suits and I will build the session around it.
Regards
Working Session: Head of Operations Search for {{fact:f:E-2018-001.client}}

The session settled the long list and left two matters open, each with an owner. It ran ninety minutes at the client's offices. This record follows the order the meeting took: who was present, the state of the market, the long list, the client's questions, and the items each of us now holds.
Present

items: Jason Vasquez, General Manager, {{fact:f:E-2018-001.client}}
James Grant, Senior Consultant, Northgate Talent Partners
Nicole Donovan, Research Associate, Northgate Talent Partners

blocks.text: The long list

The list stands at nine people in live conversation, down from ten a month ago. James Grant took the meeting through each of them by the operation they run today and the scale of it. No candidate was named in the room and none is named here.

Five of the nine were assessed as likely to reach the slate. Two are strong operators working at a smaller scale than this role carries and would be a stretch appointment on either side. The remaining two are being kept warm while their own circumstances settle, and neither has been asked for a decision yet.
What the market has said back

The specification asks for somebody who has taken an operation through a systems change and out the other side. That profile is thinner in this region than the map suggested it would be, and James Grant said so plainly rather than leave the meeting to discover it later. The people who have done it are mostly at businesses one size larger than {{fact:f:E-2018-001.client}} and will move for scope, not for money.

Jason Vasquez asked whether widening the search geographically would open the field. The meeting agreed to test that rather than assume it. Nicole Donovan will run a second pass across two adjacent markets and report what it actually turns up before anyone commits to relocation terms.
The client's questions

Jason Vasquez asked how the interview process can be built so that his own people meet the finalists without the search becoming general knowledge inside the business. James Grant proposed that every finalist meeting be held off site and that one named person on the client side hold the full list. Jason Vasquez took the choice of that person away with him.

He asked as well when he will see a slate. James Grant said October, conditional on the compensation band holding; if the band moves, the date moves with it. Jason Vasquez did not dispute the condition and asked to be told the moment the band starts to look like a problem.
Reservation recorded

Jason Vasquez is not persuaded that the two stretch candidates belong on a slate at all, and said he would rather the slate be short. The point was noted and not resolved. It comes back when the slate is drafted.
Items and owners

rows: Second research pass across the two adjacent markets
Written appraisals for the five slate-likely candidates
Name the single point of contact holding the full list
Confirm the compensation band in writing
Draft interview schedule for the finalist meetings

blocks.text: Minutes taken by Nicole Donovan. Corrections to me by the end of the week, after which this record stands as written.
Status Report: Head of Operations Search

Prepared for the leadership of {{fact:f:E-2018-001.client}} by James Grant, Senior Consultant, covering the period since our working session earlier this month. The search is at its midpoint and is on schedule for a slate in October.
Where the search stands

The research is complete across the sectors we agreed at kickoff, and the second pass over two adjacent markets closed last week, which means the target list will not grow again except by exception. Of the forty-four people approached since the specification was signed off, twenty-six took a first conversation, nine are in live conversation now, and five have been through a full assessment interview with me in person.

The arithmetic behind those numbers is worth recording, because it bears on how the remaining months should be run. The profile the specification asks for is genuinely scarce here, so the yield per approach is lower than we forecast at kickoff and each conversation takes longer to mature than it would on a role with a deeper bench behind it. That is a cost in patience rather than in money, and it sits on our side of the line.
Completed since the last report

items: 1. The second research pass closed. It produced three additional prospects, two of whom are now in conversation, and it settled the question of whether the adjacent markets hold a deeper bench, which they do not.
2. Five assessment interviews were completed in person, each with a written appraisal on file. Nobody reaches your slate without one, and the appraisals travel with the slate when it comes.
3. Nicole Donovan built and circulated the interview architecture for the finalist meetings: off site, two rounds, and one named point of contact on your side who holds the full list.
4. The compensation band was confirmed in writing on your side. That unblocked the second wave of approaches and has already changed the temperature of two conversations that had stalled on it.

blocks.text: The period ahead

items: 1. Reference work opens on the leading candidates next month, ahead of the slate rather than after it. That is not our usual sequence, and it is a deliberate response to how tight this market has proved.
2. The slate comes to you in October, with a written appraisal of each candidate on it and our reasons for setting the others aside.
3. Finalist meetings follow in November, arranged around your calendar and held away from your premises.
4. Offer and close after that. We stay with the search until your candidate has accepted and given notice to their present employer.

blocks.text: The engagement against its budget

The assignment is a fixed fee of {{fact:f:E-2018-001.fee}}, invoiced in three equal parts. The first was billed on commencement and the second falls due on delivery of the slate, so you should expect no invoice from us between now and October. Expenses are running under what we projected at kickoff, largely because most of the assessment interviews were held within a day's travel, and they appear line by line on each invoice rather than as a single figure.
Risks, and what we are doing about them

items: 1. Scarcity of the profile. Nine live conversations is a workable number and it is not a comfortable one. If two were to withdraw in the same fortnight the October date would be at risk, and you would hear that from us on the day it happened, not at the next report.

2. Counteroffers. Two of the five assessed candidates matter enough to their present employers that a counteroffer is likely, so we work that risk during references and during the offer, while there is still something to be done about it.

3. The turn of the year. The last weeks of December are effectively closed for interviewing, so any slip in November compresses into a window that will not stretch. That is the argument for holding the October date firmly rather than comfortably.

4. Confidentiality inside the business. The more people at {{fact:f:E-2018-001.client}} who know a search is running, the shorter the odds that a candidate hears about it from somewhere other than us. The single point of contact is the control on that, and it only works if it is observed.

blocks.text: What we need from you

The slate presentation is the next fixed point in the search and it needs a room rather than a telephone call, so we need two hours of your leadership team's time in the second half of October, booked now while the calendar is still open. Nicole Donovan will come to your assistant this week with three options, and taking one of them before the month is out is the single thing that keeps the November meetings where they are.
